blocks.content: Left join kept every row from the left table. Right join kept every row from the right table. Full join genuinely combines both ideas at once, keeping every row from both tables, matched or not, in a single result.

This topic covers exactly what a full join keeps, a worked example spanning customers with zero orders and orphaned orders together, distinguishing which side actually went unmatched, and how to emulate a full join on a database that lacks native support for it.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438415200-666828702.png
1. What a Full Join Actually Keeps
blocks.text: 1. What a Full Join Actually Keeps

blocks.content: A full join genuinely keeps every row from both tables involved. Where a real match exists on both sides, the row shows genuine values from both tables. Where a match exists on only one side, the columns from the missing side simply become NULL.
This means a customer with zero orders still appears, with the order columns as NULL, and an orphaned order with no valid customer still appears too, with the customer columns as NULL.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438415201-344652433.png
blocks.alt: What a Full Join Actually Keeps

blocks.content: 2. Full Join Compared To Inner, Left, and Right Join
blocks.text: 2. Full Join Compared To Inner, Left, and Right Join

blocks.content: Inner join keeps only the genuine overlap. Left join keeps the left side complete. Right join keeps the right side complete. Full join is genuinely the union of all three ideas, keeping the overlap plus the unmatched rows from both sides at once.

A useful mental model is that a full join result always contains at least as many rows as an inner join result on the same two tables, since it adds back everything inner join would have discarded from both sides.

3. A Worked Example

Suppose the customers table has a few customers who genuinely never placed an order, and the orders table has a few orphaned rows from deleted customer accounts, the same setup used for left join and right join. A full join surfaces every one of these cases together in a single query.

Every customer appears, even ones with zero orders, showing NULL for amount. Every order appears too, even orphaned ones, showing NULL for name. A full join is genuinely the only single join type that surfaces both problems in one query.

4. Finding Rows That Exist On Only One Side
blocks.text: 4. Finding Rows That Exist On Only One Side

blocks.content: Because a full join can produce three genuinely distinct outcomes per row, a matched pair, a customer with no orders, or an orphaned order, checking which specific column is NULL tells you exactly which case you are looking at.

SELECT c.id, o.id
FROM customers c
FULL JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id
WHERE c.id IS NULL OR o.id IS NULL;
blocks.code:
SELECT c.id, o.id
FROM customers c
FULL JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id
WHERE c.id IS NULL OR o.id IS NULL;

codes.sql:
SELECT c.id, o.id
FROM customers c
FULL JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id
WHERE c.id IS NULL OR o.id IS NULL;

blocks.content: This query isolates every row that is genuinely unmatched on either side, customers with zero orders together with orphaned orders, in a single pass over both tables.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438415522-634538146.png
blocks.alt: Finding Rows That Exist On Only One Side

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A row where neither c.id nor o.id is NULL represents a genuine match on both sides. Only check the columns you actually expect could be missing, not every column in the row.
5. Full Join Without Native Support

Some widely used databases, including MySQL, genuinely do not support FULL JOIN as a keyword at all. On these databases, the same result is built by running a left join and a right join separately, then combining them with UNION.

UNION genuinely removes duplicate rows between the two halves, which is exactly what is needed here, since matched rows would otherwise appear once from the left join half and once again from the right join half.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438415523-24769313.png

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: UNION ALL keeps duplicates instead of removing them. Using UNION ALL here would genuinely double every matched row, since it appears in both the left join half and the right join half.
6. Genuinely Common Mistakes

A few real patterns undermine full join usage. Using UNION ALL instead of UNION when emulating a full join, which duplicates every genuinely matched row. Assuming every database supports the FULL JOIN keyword natively, then hitting a syntax error on one that does not.
And forgetting that a full join result can contain NULLs from either table, then writing later filters or calculations that silently break on rows where the expected column turned out to be NULL.
